lead: Efficiency alone does not tell you how big an engine must be. Two cycles with the same efficiency can give very different work per stroke. The mean effective pressure (MEP) measures that: it is the steady pressure that, pushing the piston over one full stroke, would give the cycle's net work. A high MEP means a small, light engine for the power. This chapter defines the MEP, uses it to find engine power, and compares the Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles on the bases examiners use: the same compression ratio, the same peak pressure and temperature, and the same heat input.
prereq: You need the three cycles and their efficiency formulas from Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles.

sections.h3: Mean effective pressure and engine power

blocks.text: Per kg of air, the swept volume is v₁ − v₂ (largest minus smallest specific volume). The MEP is the net work divided by it:

Here w<sub>net</sub> is in kJ/kg and v in m³/kg, so p<sub>m</sub> comes out in kPa; W<sub>net</sub> is the net work per cycle in kJ and V<sub>s</sub> the swept volume in m³. Since v₂ = v₁/r, the swept volume is v₁(1 − 1/r). For the Otto cycle this gives a closed formula:

The MEP turns a cycle into engine power. Power = p<sub>m</sub> × V<sub>s</sub> × (cycles per second) × (number of cylinders). A four-stroke engine completes one cycle in two revolutions, so cycles per second = N/120 with N in rpm; a two-stroke engine completes one per revolution, N/60.

sections.h3: Comparing Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles

blocks.text: Every comparison starts from one fact: η = 1 − q<sub>out</sub>/q<sub>in</sub>, and in all three cycles the heat is rejected along the same kind of constant-volume line from the end of expansion back to state 1. On the T-s diagram q<sub>out</sub> is the area under that line, so the cycle that ends its heat addition at the smaller entropy rejects less heat.

Same compression ratio and same heat input. States 1 and 2 are shared. A constant-volume line on T-s is steeper than a constant-pressure line, so to take in the same heat (the same area under the line) the Otto cycle climbs high with little entropy rise, and the Diesel cycle runs further to the right. The Diesel cycle then rejects more heat. Its temperature rises all through the constant-pressure heat addition (q = cpΔT with ΔT > 0), but it reaches a lower peak, so the mean temperature at which heat enters is lower. Result: ηOtto > ηDual > ηDiesel.

Same peak pressure and peak temperature. Now state 3 is shared and the heat rejected is the same. The Diesel cycle can reach that peak pressure with a much higher compression ratio, so it takes in more heat for the same rejection. Result: ηDiesel > ηDual > ηOtto. The same order holds for the same peak pressure and the same heat input. This is the fair comparison for real engines, because peak pressure is what the cylinder and bearings must withstand.

The mean temperature idea gives the same answers in one line. Write T<sub>m,in</sub> = q<sub>in</sub>/Δs for the heat addition and T<sub>m,out</sub> = q<sub>out</sub>/Δs for the rejection, with the same Δs for both because the cycle closes; then η = 1 − T<sub>m,out</sub>/T<sub>m,in</sub>, and the cycle with the higher mean temperature of heat addition wins on that basis.

examples.question: An air standard Dual cycle has a compression ratio of 14. At the start of compression the air is at 1 bar and 300 K. The pressure ratio during constant-volume heat addition is 1.5 and the cut-off ratio is 1.6. Take c<sub>p</sub> = 1.005, c<sub>v</sub> = 0.718, R = 0.287 kJ/kg·K and γ = 1.4. Find the temperatures, the heat added and rejected, the efficiency and the mean effective pressure.
steps: Constant volume: T₃ = 1.5 × 862.1 = 1293.2 K and p₃ = 1.5 × 40.23 = 60.35 bar (the peak pressure).
Constant pressure: T₄ = 1.6 × 1293.2 = 2069.1 K (the peak temperature).
Expansion to v₅ = v₁: T₅ = T₁r<sub>p</sub>r<sub>c</sub><sup>γ</sup> = 300 × 1.5 × 1.931 = 868.9 K.

examples.question: A four-cylinder four-stroke petrol engine has a bore of 80 mm and a stroke of 90 mm and runs at 3000 rpm. Its air standard cycle is the Otto cycle of the worked example in Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles (r = 8, 800 kJ/kg added, w<sub>net</sub> = 451.8 kJ/kg). Find the MEP and the air standard power.
steps: MEP: v₁ − v₂ = 0.861 − 0.1076 = 0.7534 m³/kg, so p<sub>m</sub> = 451.8/0.7534 = 599.7 kPa, about 6.0 bar. The closed formula with r<sub>p</sub> = 48.09/18.38 = 2.617 gives the same 599 kPa.
Swept volume of one cylinder: V<sub>s</sub> = (π/4) × 0.08² × 0.09 = 4.524 × 10⁻⁴ m³.
examples.answer: MEP = 6.0 bar; air standard power = 27.1 kW. The engine's real indicated power is lower, because the real cycle has a smaller area than the air standard loop.

traps: MEP uses the swept volume v₁ − v₂, not v₁. Dividing 680.8 by 0.861 gives 7.91 bar instead of 8.52 bar.
In a four-stroke engine the number of cycles per minute is N/2, not N. Using N doubles the power.
"Otto is more efficient than Diesel" is true only for the same compression ratio and heat input. For the same peak pressure the order reverses. State the basis before you compare.

During constant-pressure heat addition the temperature keeps rising. The Diesel cycle loses at equal r because it ends its heat addition at a larger entropy, so it rejects more heat, not because the gas cools.
A higher efficiency does not mean a higher MEP. The Carnot cycle has the highest efficiency and one of the lowest MEPs.

quiz.a: The constant pressure which, acting on the piston over one full stroke, would do the same net work as the cycle: p<sub>m</sub> = w<sub>net</sub>/(v₁ − v₂).

quiz.q: For the same compression ratio and heat input, arrange the Otto, Diesel and Dual cycles by efficiency and give the reason.
quiz.a: Otto > Dual > Diesel. With states 1 and 2 shared, the steeper constant-volume line takes in the heat with less entropy rise, so less heat is rejected along the constant-volume line back to state 1.

quiz.q: Why is the comparison at the same peak pressure the fair one for real engines?
quiz.a: Peak pressure sets the strength and weight of the cylinder, head and bearings. An engine is designed to a pressure limit, and at that limit the Diesel cycle's higher compression ratio wins.

quiz.q: An Otto cycle gives w<sub>net</sub> = 500 kJ/kg with v₁ = 0.86 m³/kg and r = 9. Find the MEP.
A single-cylinder two-stroke engine has a swept volume of 0.5 L, an MEP of 7 bar and runs at 2400 rpm. Find its power.
In the Dual example, the pressure ratio rises from 1.5 to 2.0 with r<sub>c</sub> still 1.6. Without full working, say what happens to η and to the MEP, and why.
quiz.a: Both rise. More heat goes in at constant volume near top dead centre, at the full expansion ratio, which raises the mean temperature of heat addition and the net work; the swept volume is unchanged, so the MEP rises with the work.

quiz.q: Using the table, explain why the Diesel cycle wins at equal peak pressure even though it loses at equal compression ratio.
quiz.a: At equal peak pressure (60 bar) the Diesel cycle runs at r = 18.6 against 9.0 for Otto. The heat rejected is the same (380.9 kJ/kg in both, since state 3 is shared), but the Diesel cycle takes in more heat, so its efficiency is higher: 63.3% against 58.5%.

beyond: Engine makers quote brake mean effective pressure (BMEP), which uses the shaft work instead of the cycle work; modern turbocharged diesel engines reach BMEP values several times those of older naturally aspirated ones. Cycle comparisons with variable specific heats and combustion timing are done in engine simulation software. To go further, search for "brake mean effective pressure", "engine downsizing turbocharging" and "finite-time thermodynamics engine".

figure.caption: Otto and Diesel cycles with the same compression ratio (14) and the same heat input (1200 kJ/kg) share states 1 and 2. The steeper constant-volume line takes the heat in with less rise in entropy, so the Otto cycle rejects less heat (the area under its line 4-1) than the Diesel cycle (which adds the right-hand strip).
